Albert Park Grand Prix Circuit.name: Albert Park Circuit
Albert Park Grand Prix Circuit.history: Set amid the tranquil parkland of Melbourne's Albert Park, this semi-permanent street circuit winds through public roads around the lake. It has hosted the Australian Grand Prix since 1996 and traditionally opens the F1 season. The circuit was heavily modified in 2021 and 2022 to improve overtaking, resulting in faster lap times and more on-track action.

Bahrain International Circuit.name: Bahrain International Circuit
Bahrain International Circuit.history: Built in the desert on the outskirts of Sakhir, Bahrain's purpose-built circuit made history as the first Grand Prix held in the Middle East. Designed by Hermann Tilke, it features wide run-off areas and a long pit straight. The track can also be configured as the shorter 'Outer Circuit', used for the 2020 Sakhir GP. It is consistently praised for producing close racing.

Jeddah Corniche Circuit.name: Jeddah Corniche Circuit
Jeddah Corniche Circuit.history: Stretching along the Red Sea Corniche, the Jeddah Street Circuit is F1's fastest street circuit, with average speeds exceeding 250 km/h. Despite being temporary, it features 27 corners — many of them high-speed and blind — making it one of the most technically demanding circuits on the calendar. It debuted in 2021 and has already produced several dramatic and controversial races.

Suzuka International Racing Course.name: Suzuka Circuit
Suzuka International Racing Course.history: Universally beloved by drivers and fans alike, Suzuka is one of the most iconic circuits in motorsport. Its distinctive figure-of-eight layout, created by crossing an overpass, includes legendary sections like the Esses, Degner Curve, and the ultra-fast 130R corner. Built by Honda in 1962, it has hosted the Japanese Grand Prix almost continuously since 1987 and has been the scene of many championship-deciding moments.

Shanghai International Circuit.name: Shanghai International Circuit
Shanghai International Circuit.history: Shanghai's circuit is immediately recognisable for its snail-shaped Turn 1-2 complex and a long back straight that creates excellent overtaking opportunities. Designed by Hermann Tilke, it opened alongside Bahrain in 2004 as F1 expanded into Asia. The Chinese Grand Prix was absent from the calendar from 2020 to 2023 due to COVID-19 restrictions, returning in 2024.

Miami International Autodrome.name: Miami International Autodrome
Miami International Autodrome.history: Built in the carpark surrounding the Hard Rock Stadium, this Hermann Tilke-designed circuit debuted in 2022. It features a fake marina section and a mix of slow technical corners and high-speed blasts. Despite its manufactured setting, the Miami GP quickly became one of the most popular events on the calendar, drawing massive celebrity interest and passionate crowds.

Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari.name: Autodromo di Imola
Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari.history: Named after Enzo Ferrari and his son Dino, this circuit on the banks of the Santerno River has a hallowed place in motorsport history. It was here that Ayrton Senna and Roland Ratzenberger lost their lives in 1994. The circuit has been extensively modified for safety since then and returned to the F1 calendar in 2020 after a 14-year absence.

Circuit de Monaco.name: Circuit de Monaco
Circuit de Monaco.history: The crown jewel of Formula 1, Monaco winds through the narrow streets of the tiny principality on the Côte d'Azur. With virtually no run-off, armco barriers inches from the car, and a tunnel section, it is F1's most glamorous and most unforgiving circuit. Winning Monaco is considered the pinnacle of a driver's career. The circuit has changed remarkably little since the first Monaco Grand Prix in 1929.

Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya.name: Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya
Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya.history: Built on the outskirts of Barcelona to replace the old Montjuïc street circuit, the Circuit de Catalunya has been a fixture on the F1 calendar since 1991. Known for its demanding high-speed corners, it has long been F1 teams' preferred pre-season testing location. The circuit was updated with a new layout at Turn 10 in 2004 and again in 2021.

Circuit Gilles Villeneuve.name: Circuit Gilles Villeneuve
Circuit Gilles Villeneuve.history: Named after the beloved Canadian driver Gilles Villeneuve who died in 1982, this semi-permanent circuit is laid out on the Île Notre-Dame in the St. Lawrence River. The 'Wall of Champions' at the final chicane has claimed countless title challengers. The Canadian GP is famous for its unpredictable weather, safety car appearances, and uniquely festive atmosphere.

Red Bull Ring.name: Red Bull Ring
Red Bull Ring.history: Nestled in the green hills of Styria, the Red Bull Ring has one of the most dramatic natural settings in F1. Originally built in 1969 as the Österreichring, it was redeveloped by Helmut Marko and Dietrich Mateschitz in 2011. With only ten corners, it is F1's shortest circuit and places a heavy emphasis on engine power and aerodynamic efficiency.

Silverstone Circuit.name: Silverstone Circuit
Silverstone Circuit.history: Converted from a WWII RAF airfield, Silverstone held the very first Formula 1 World Championship race in 1950. The circuit has evolved enormously since then but retains its high-speed character, with legendary corners including Copse, Maggots, Becketts, and Chapel. The British Grand Prix consistently draws the largest crowds on the F1 calendar.

Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps.name: Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps
Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps.history: Cutting through the Ardennes forest in southern Belgium, Spa-Francorchamps is widely regarded as the greatest racing circuit in the world. Its combination of fast corners — including the iconic Eau Rouge/Raidillon — long straights, and notoriously unpredictable weather make it a supreme test of driver and car. The circuit has existed since 1921 and was extensively rebuilt in 2022.

Hungaroring.name: Hungaroring
Hungaroring.history: Built in a natural amphitheatre outside Budapest in just eight months, the Hungaroring hosted the first Formula 1 race behind the Iron Curtain in 1986. Its twisty, narrow layout offers few overtaking opportunities and places a premium on qualifying pace. Often compared to Monaco without the barriers, it rewards precision rather than raw speed.

Circuit Zandvoort.name: Circuit Zandvoort
Circuit Zandvoort.history: Set in the sand dunes of the North Sea coast, Zandvoort is one of Europe's most atmospheric circuits. After a 35-year absence, it returned to the F1 calendar in 2021 following renovations including the addition of banked corners — the first in F1 since Indianapolis. The Dutch Grand Prix has become one of the calendar's most popular events, with a sea of orange Verstappen fans creating an extraordinary atmosphere.

Autodromo Nazionale di Monza.name: Autodromo Nazionale Monza
Autodromo Nazionale di Monza.history: Known as the 'Temple of Speed', Monza is the fastest circuit on the F1 calendar and one of the oldest in the world. Built in 1922 and set in a stunning royal park north of Milan, it hosts the Italian Grand Prix and is the spiritual home of Scuderia Ferrari. The tifosi turn every race into an unforgettable spectacle.

Baku City Circuit.name: Baku City Circuit
Baku City Circuit.history: Running through the ancient streets of Azerbaijan's capital and along the Caspian Sea Boulevard, Baku is a circuit of contrasts. The narrow castle section features a hairpin wider than the road itself, while the main straight is nearly 2.2 km long — the longest in F1. Since its debut in 2016, it has produced some of the most chaotic and dramatic races in recent F1 history.

Marina Bay Street Circuit.name: Marina Bay Street Circuit
Marina Bay Street Circuit.history: The Singapore Grand Prix was F1's first-ever night race when it debuted in 2008, lit by over 1,500 floodlights illuminating the Marina Bay skyline. The circuit weaves through the heart of Singapore's financial district, passing iconic landmarks including the Marina Bay Sands hotel. It is one of the most physically demanding events on the calendar, combining heat, humidity, and a relentlessly technical layout.

Circuit of the Americas.name: Circuit of the Americas
Circuit of the Americas.history: Built from scratch in the Texas Hill Country south of Austin, COTA was designed to bring F1 back to the United States on a permanent basis. Hermann Tilke incorporated elements of famous circuits from around the world, including a replica of Silverstone's Maggots-Becketts sequence. The circuit opened in 2012 and is widely praised as one of the best modern circuits.

Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.name: Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez
Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.history: Named after brothers Ricardo and Pedro Rodriguez, who both lost their lives racing, this circuit in Mexico City sits at 2,240 metres altitude — the highest on the F1 calendar. The thin air significantly reduces aerodynamic downforce and engine cooling efficiency. A stadium section built inside the Foro Sol baseball stadium creates one of F1's most electric atmospheres.

Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace.name: Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace
Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace.history: Named after the Brazilian driver Carlos Pace who died in a plane crash in 1977, Interlagos is one of F1's most beloved circuits. Its anti-clockwise layout and the thunderous Senna S — named after Brazil's greatest driver — make it unique. The circuit's raw emotional character, surrounded by a working-class neighbourhood of São Paulo, gives it an atmosphere unlike anywhere else on the calendar.

Las Vegas Strip Street Circuit.name: Las Vegas Strip Circuit
Las Vegas Strip Street Circuit.history: Formula 1's most theatrical venue, the Las Vegas Strip Street Circuit runs past the world-famous casino resorts including the Bellagio, MGM Grand, and Caesars Palace. The race is held at night under the spectacular neon lights of the Strip. F1 previously raced in Las Vegas in 1981 and 1982 in the Caesars Palace car park, but the modern event is on an entirely different scale.

Losail International Circuit.name: Losail International Circuit
Losail International Circuit.history: Originally built for MotoGP, the Lusail Circuit became part of the F1 calendar in 2021 and became a permanent fixture from 2023 as part of Qatar's 10-year deal with Formula 1. A smooth, flowing layout with sweeping high-speed corners makes it a driver favourite. The race is held under floodlights, creating a spectacular visual backdrop.

Yas Marina Circuit.name: Yas Marina Circuit
Yas Marina Circuit.history: Built on Yas Island in Abu Dhabi's coastal waters, this Hermann Tilke-designed circuit closes the F1 season each year and has hosted several championship deciders. A comprehensive redesign in 2021 transformed the final sector into a flowing, high-speed section that dramatically improved racing. The Viceroy Hotel famously straddles the circuit's pitlane exit.

Sepang International Circuit.name: Sepang International Circuit
Sepang International Circuit.history: Designed by Hermann Tilke and opened in 1999, Sepang was the prototype for almost every Tilke circuit that followed and hosted the Malaysian Grand Prix from 1999 to 2017. Known for brutal tropical heat, sudden monsoon downpours, and an abrasive surface that chews through tyres, it returns to the F1 calendar for 2026 as a substitute venue after the Bahrain Grand Prix was relocated there.

Circuito de Madring.name: Circuito de Madring
Circuito de Madring.history: Built around the IFEMA exhibition centre in the Valdebebas district, Madring marks Formula 1's return to Madrid for the first time since Circuito del Jarama in 1981. The hybrid street/permanent layout features La Monumental, a 550-metre corner banked at 24 degrees — the steepest permitted under current regulations. Its 2026 debut makes Spain the third country on the calendar, alongside Italy and the USA, to host two Grands Prix in one season.
